[1] rewrite

```
- **Why 0.5%.** No record says how it was chosen. It dates from an earlier,
  approximate method, whose runs differed by about 0.04% in the alveolar
  concentration and by more in mixed venous. The test also requires each gap in
  gas fraction to stay below 1e-14. A gap less than 1e-8 meets the 0.5% limit
  whatever its percentage, so every gap that fails the 0.5% limit fails the
  1e-14 limit too. Today the 0.5% limit changes no outcome.
```

[2] rewrite

```
- **How to change it.** A fork with an approximate method fails the 1e-14 limit
  even when its arithmetic is correct. For example, a first-order method shows
  gaps near 1.4e-11. Relax the 1e-14 limit, and the 0.5% limit then decides the
  test's result. Set the 0.5% limit above your method's gaps at the three steps
  and below a difference that a learner could see. The limits are in
  `tests/reference/test_sevo_patient.py`.
```

[3] rewrite

```
**The release check, and why it allows 0.5%.** The model advances in fixed
steps of 0.1 s. A shorter step should give almost the same result. Before
each release, a test reruns the first minute of the default sevoflurane
induction with steps of 0.1 s, 0.05 s and 0.025 s. Each run's alveolar,
vessel-rich and mixed-venous concentrations must be within 0.5% of the run with
the next shorter step. A compartment that holds almost no agent also passes if
its values in the two runs differ by less than 0.000001 vol%, because there a
tiny difference is a large percentage. The 0.5% limit was set for the
simulator's earlier calculation method, at about ten times the 0.04% alveolar
difference that method showed. The current method's runs agree to better than
one part in a trillion (checked 2026-10-03), so the much tighter limits in the
paragraphs above are the ones that would catch a real error.
```

[4] rewrite

```
The 5e-3 relative tolerance was chosen when the simulator used an earlier,
approximate method (an operator split). That method showed a relative gap of
4e-4 in the alveolar fraction between steps of 0.1 s and 0.025 s, and 5e-3 is
about ten times that gap. With the current, exact method, the same comparison
gives relative gaps of about 1.4e-13 (checked 2026-10-03), so the tolerance is
kept only as a coarse check. For a fraction so close to zero that a relative
gap means little, any gap less than the 1e-8 absolute tolerance also passes.
```

[5] rewrite

```
**The release check, and why it allows 0.5%.** The simulator moves the model
forward in fixed time steps, normally 0.1 s long. A shorter step should give
almost the same result. If it does not, the step is too long. Before each
release, a test runs the first minute of the default sevoflurane induction
three times, with steps of 0.1 s, 0.05 s and 0.025 s. In each run, the
alveolar, vessel-rich and mixed-venous concentrations must be within 0.5% of
the run with the next shorter step. A compartment that still holds almost no
agent also passes if its values in the two runs differ by less than
0.000001 vol%, because there a tiny difference can be a large percentage. The
0.5% limit was set for the simulator's earlier calculation method, whose 0.1 s
and 0.025 s runs differed by about 0.04% in alveolar concentration. With the
current method, the three runs agree to better than one part in a trillion
(checked 2026-10-03), so the 0.5% limit is now only a coarse safety net. The
much tighter limit in the paragraphs above is the one that would catch a real
error.
```
